newsitem.title: USA: Texaco shares hit high as shareholders meet.
newsitem.headline: Texaco shares hit high as shareholders meet.

text.p: Texaco Inc. shares hit a record high as the company held its annual meeting Tuesday, a reward, Chief Executive Officer Peter Bijur told shareholders, for strong financial performance.

Bijur also sought to restore the company's image after it was tarnished by transcripts of tapes on which company executives allegedly talked about destroying documents and made racist remarks in regard to a lawsuit last year by 1,400 blacks and other minorities.
"The behaviour and tone of the tapes affected us all," Bijur told shareholders, noting the company settled the suit to avoid a lengthy and potentially more costly court battle.
Texaco says the settlement was worth $115 million while plaintiffs value it at $176 million, which would be the biggest ever in a discrimination case in the United States.

Bijur said the company was well on the way to meeting employment targets for women and minorities and that 49 percent of new hires in the first quarter of 1997 were women and 36 percent were minorities.
Texaco also has spent $36.3 million with women and minority businesses and plans a total of $175 million for 1997. No comparative or total spending figures were available.
"We have vowed within Texaco to eradicate any prejudice and racial intolerance," Bijur said.
While Bijur was congratulated on progress, pressure groups criticised Texaco for not accepting motions on diversity on the board and voting on board members each year.
"We want to cooperate with you, but we think your company is a test case for so many," said Sister Barbara of the Congress of Sisters of Charity for the Incarnate Word.
The Reverend Jesse Jackson said the continued employment and even promotion of managers who had been involved in discrimination marred the progress that Texaco was making.

He noted the proposed merger of Texaco's domestic refining and marketing units in the United States with Shell Oil Co., a unit of Royal Dutch/Shell Group, posed questions about equality as Shell faces race and sex discrimination suits.
The company also was criticised for its involvement in a natural gas field 125 miles off the coast of Burma, which human rights activists say aids the country's military regime.
"Is the financial prize so powerful that we have to relinquish our soul," said Father Joe LaMar of the Interfaith Centre on Corporate Responsibility, a church investment body.
While rejecting any explicit link between human rights and Texaco, Bijur said the company was evaluating its 43 percent stake in the field.

"We have prepared and circulated financial data and project background information to see if other options -- such as a sale or swap with another company -- would yield better value," Bijur told shareholders.
Texaco's alleged pollution of the rainforest in Ecuador also came under attack in connection with a lawsuit seeking $1 billion for the alleged spilling of 17 million gallons of oil.
Bijur said Texaco had fully met its responsibilities in Ecuador and had completed a major cleanup in cooperation with the government and state oil company.
Texaco stock hit a high of $113.50 but later gave the gains back and closed off 75 cents at $111.875 on the New York Stock Exchange.
